w92.bptypes: Bipolar I vs II vs cyclothymic

BANK.q: A client's BP is 120/60 mmHg. What is the mean arterial pressure (MAP)?
BANK.r: MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3 = (120 + 120) ÷ 3 = 80 mmHg. Normal MAP is about 70–100; at least 65 supports vital-organ perfusion.

BANK.q: Which bedside findings support ADEQUATE tissue perfusion? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Perfusion anchors: MAP ≥65, urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr, cap refill <3 sec, and normal mentation. A change in mentation can be an early sign of falling cerebral perfusion.

BANK.q: Which finding is often the EARLIEST sign of falling cerebral perfusion?
BANK.r: The slides list mentation as the earliest sign of falling cerebral perfusion. Watch for new restlessness, anxiety or confusion.

BANK.q: Which description matches an aortic dissection?
o: Permanent dilation of all three wall layers
An intimal tear lets blood track between wall layers, creating a false lumen
A wall disruption contained by surrounding soft tissue
A berry-shaped outpouching on one side of a cerebral artery
BANK.r: Dissection = intimal tear + false lumen; an acute, highly lethal emergency. A true aneurysm is dilation with an intact, stretched wall. A pseudoaneurysm is a wall disruption contained by tissue.

BANK.q: A client develops a pulsatile mass at the femoral puncture site after a cardiac catheterization. The wall is disrupted and the leak is contained by soft tissue. This is a:
BANK.r: Pseudoaneurysm: wall disrupted; leaked blood contained by surrounding tissue. Typically post-procedural or traumatic.

BANK.q: Which aneurysm shape is uniform circumferential dilation typical of the abdominal aorta?
BANK.r: Fusiform = uniform circumferential dilation (abdominal aorta). Saccular = outpouching on one side (cerebral berry aneurysm).

BANK.q: According to Laplace's law, which client has the HIGHEST aneurysm wall tension?
BANK.r: Wall tension = Pressure × Radius. The largest aneurysm with the highest BP has the most wall tension and the greatest rupture risk. This is why BP control is central.

BANK.q: Which factors weaken the arterial wall and contribute to aneurysm formation? Select all that apply.
o: Proteolytic enzymes degrading elastin and collagen
BANK.r: Chronic HTN + turbulent flow stress the wall; inflammation/proteolytic enzymes degrade elastin and collagen; atherosclerosis stiffens and weakens it. Once dilation starts, it becomes self-perpetuating.

BANK.q: Why does a larger aneurysm rupture more often even if BP stays the same?
o: Larger aneurysms always have higher BP
A wider radius raises wall tension at the same pressure
BANK.r: Laplace: tension = pressure × radius. As the diameter grows, wall tension rises even at the same BP, so dilation is self-perpetuating.

BANK.q: Which is the single strongest MODIFIABLE risk factor for aneurysm?
BANK.r: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk. Smoking cessation + BP control are the two interventions that most change the trajectory. Age, sex and family history are non-modifiable.

BANK.q: Which are NON-modifiable risk factors for aneurysm? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Non-modifiable: age >60, male sex (AAA), family history, connective tissue disease (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos), female sex for cerebral rupture. Stimulants and HTN are modifiable.

BANK.q: Which statement about sex and aneurysm risk matches the lecture?
o: Male sex is common for AAA; female sex increases cerebral aneurysm rupture risk
Sex has no effect on aneurysm risk
Male sex increases cerebral rupture risk only
BANK.r: AAA is more common in males; female sex raises cerebral aneurysm rupture risk.

BANK.q: A client with a known 5.0 cm AAA is admitted. Which nursing action is CONTRAINDICATED?
o: Deep, repeated palpation of the abdomen
BANK.r: Do NOT deeply or repeatedly palpate a suspected or known AAA; it can precipitate rupture.

BANK.q: Which findings are classic for a stable abdominal aortic aneurysm? Select all that apply.
o: Pulsatile mass at or above the umbilicus
Steady, deep back or flank pain
BANK.r: AAA: often silent; when present, pulsatile mass at/above umbilicus, bruit, steady deep back/flank pain. Hoarseness = TAA; mass behind knee = popliteal.

BANK.q: Elective repair of an AAA is generally considered when the aneurysm reaches:
o: 5.5 cm or growth >0.5 cm in 6 months
BANK.r: Normal aorta 2–3 cm. Repair threshold ≈5.5 cm or rapid growth >0.5 cm in 6 months. Under 5.5 cm: surveillance imaging, BP/lipid control, smoking cessation.

BANK.q: A client with a known AAA reports NEW back pain. What should the nurse assume?
o: Muscle strain from lying in bed
BANK.r: New back pain in a known AAA is rupture until proven otherwise. Rupture triad: sudden severe pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass.

BANK.q: A client has a thoracic aortic aneurysm. Which findings are caused by compression of nearby structures? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: TAA: hoarseness (laryngeal nerve compression), dysphagia (esophagus), dyspnea (airway). Pain is deep, diffuse chest or upper back.

BANK.q: A client with a TAA has BP 168/92 in the right arm and 132/80 in the left. What does the nurse suspect?
BANK.r: Unequal BP between arms suggests dissection. TAA complications: rupture, dissection, aortic regurgitation, thromboembolism.

BANK.q: Which pain pattern fits a thoracic aortic aneurysm?
o: Wave-like flank pain radiating to the groin
Deep, diffuse chest or upper-back pain
BANK.r: TAA = deep, diffuse chest or upper-back pain, plus hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea from compression.

BANK.q: A client has a popliteal aneurysm. Which finding is the PRIORITY to report?
o: Cool, pale foot with absent pedal pulse
BANK.r: Peripheral aneurysms threaten downstream perfusion. Thromboembolism → pain, pallor, diminished/absent pulse, limb ischemia. A pulsatile mass (often bilateral) is the expected finding.

BANK.q: Which complications can a popliteal aneurysm cause? Select all that apply.
o: Numbness or weakness from nerve compression
BANK.r: Popliteal: most common peripheral aneurysm; mural thrombus → ischemia; vein compression → edema; nerve compression → numbness/weakness; rupture → limb loss.

BANK.q: For any peripheral aneurysm, what is the key question for nursing assessment?
o: Is the limb downstream getting blood?
Is the BP in the left arm higher?
BANK.r: Think downstream perfusion: color, temperature, cap refill, sensation and pulses distal to the aneurysm.

BANK.q: Which test is used to SCREEN for and serially size an AAA, with no contrast?
BANK.r: Abdominal ultrasound: noninvasive, no contrast, used for screening and surveillance. CT angiography is the gold standard for size/shape/surgical planning.

BANK.q: Before a CT angiography, what should the nurse do? Select all that apply.
o: Palpate the AAA to mark its edges
BANK.r: CTA uses contrast: check renal function and allergy, and hydrate. Never palpate a known AAA.

BANK.q: Why is a type and crossmatch kept current for a symptomatic aneurysm client?
o: To prepare for possible transfusion with rupture or surgery
BANK.r: Type & screen/crossmatch prepares for transfusion (slides: crossmatch 4–6 units PRBC). CBC gives baseline H/H; renal panel is a baseline before contrast.

BANK.q: Which imaging is an alternative for a client with renal impairment or severe contrast allergy?
BANK.r: MRA maps vessels and flow without radiation and is the alternative when CTA is limited by renal function or contrast allergy.

BANK.q: Which findings suggest a RUPTURED aneurysm? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden, severe, tearing pain radiating to the back
Warm, dry skin and alert mentation
BANK.r: Ruptured: sudden severe tearing pain, hypotension + narrow pulse pressure, tachycardia, cool/pale/diaphoretic skin, restlessness → confusion, possible flank ecchymosis. Intact: warm/dry, alert, often hypertensive.

BANK.q: A client with a known AAA is restless, HR 118, skin cool and clammy, BP 124/88. What is the best interpretation?
BANK.r: Compensated shock can hide behind a normal BP. Early: restlessness, tachycardia, cool clammy skin. Do not wait for hypotension; trend mentation, pulses, skin, UO, HR and pulse pressure.

BANK.q: Which finding marks PROGRESSIVE (not early) hemorrhagic shock?
o: Hypotension, narrow pulse pressure, oliguria, confusion
BANK.r: Early: restlessness, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, normal BP. Progressive: hypotension, narrow pulse pressure, oliguria, confusion. Irreversible: profound hypotension, anuria, MODS.

BANK.q: What is the chain of events after aneurysm rupture?
o: ↓ volume → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output → ↓ MAP → organ hypoperfusion
BANK.r: Rupture → blood loss → ↓ intravascular volume → ↓ preload → ↓ CO → ↓ MAP → organs lose perfusion. Body compensates with tachycardia, vasoconstriction and narrowed pulse pressure.

BANK.q: For a stable aneurysm under 5.5 cm, which medication class is first-line to reduce HR and force of ejection?
o: Beta blockers such as labetalol or esmolol
BANK.r: Beta blockers (labetalol, esmolol) are first line; HR goal 60–70. ACE inhibitors, ARBs or CCBs are second line. Course SBP target for stable aneurysm ≈100–120.

BANK.q: A client with a ruptured AAA is awaiting emergency repair. Which SBP target does the lecture describe?
BANK.r: Permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90) limits bleeding while maintaining vital-organ perfusion before repair. Stable aneurysm target is SBP 100–120.

BANK.q: Which belong in conservative management of a small, stable aneurysm? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid heavy lifting, straining and Valsalva
Heavy weight training to build core strength
BANK.r: Conservative: BP control (cornerstone), beta blocker, statin/antiplatelet as appropriate, smoking cessation, serial imaging q6–12 months, avoid lifting/straining/Valsalva.

BANK.q: A client is 2 days post-EVAR. Which complication is SPECIFIC to EVAR and requires lifelong surveillance imaging?
BANK.r: EVAR = endoleak (persistent blood flow into the sac). Open repair = cross-clamp ischemia (kidney, bowel, spinal cord) and greater physiologic stress.

BANK.q: Compared with open repair, which are true of EVAR? Select all that apply.
o: Stent graft advanced through the femoral artery
Aorta is cross-clamped and graft sewn in
Monitor groin site and distal pulses
BANK.r: EVAR: femoral approach, shorter stay, less blood loss, monitor groin site/distal pulses/renal function, endoleak risk. Cross-clamping is open repair.

BANK.q: After OPEN repair with prolonged aortic cross-clamping, which organs are at risk for ischemia?
BANK.r: Prolonged cross-clamp → ischemic injury to kidney, spinal cord and bowel. Monitor graft patency and downstream organ perfusion.

BANK.q: Which pre-op actions are appropriate for a client with a symptomatic AAA? Select all that apply.
o: Palpate and mark peripheral pulses for baseline
Provide stool softeners and avoid Valsalva
BANK.r: Pre-op: calm, bed rest during acute pain, treat pain/anxiety (both raise BP), arterial line BP titration, mark pulses, avoid deep palpation and Valsalva, two large-bore IVs, current type & crossmatch.

BANK.q: Why does the nurse treat pain and anxiety before aneurysm repair?
o: Both raise BP, increasing wall tension
BANK.r: Pain and anxiety both raise BP. Higher pressure = more wall tension = higher rupture risk.

BANK.q: Which IV infusion might be titrated by protocol to keep BP in range pre-op?
BANK.r: Slides: titrate antihypertensive infusions such as nicardipine per protocol with continuous arterial line monitoring.

BANK.q: Post-op aneurysm repair, the client's right pedal pulse is newly absent and the foot is cool. What does the nurse suspect?
BANK.r: New absent pulse = graft occlusion/ischemia until proven otherwise. Check distal pulses, color, temp and sensation at least hourly; report change immediately.

BANK.q: After thoracic aortic repair, the client cannot move or feel the legs. Which complication is likely?
BANK.r: Spinal cord ischemia/paraplegia can follow thoracic repair. Assess leg movement and sensation.

BANK.q: Post-op aneurysm repair, which findings require prompt follow-up? Select all that apply.
o: Urine output 15 mL/hr in a 70-kg client
Increasing abdominal girth and falling Hgb
Bloody stool with severe abdominal pain
BANK.r: UO <0.5 mL/kg/hr (35 mL/hr for 70 kg) = renal hypoperfusion. Rising girth/falling Hgb = bleeding. Bloody stool + severe pain = bowel ischemia. HTN stresses the graft; hypotension risks graft thrombosis.

BANK.q: Why must post-op BP stay in the ordered window?
o: Hypertension stresses the graft; hypotension risks graft thrombosis
BANK.r: Both extremes harm the graft: HTN stresses suture lines; hypotension risks thrombosis.

BANK.q: Which discharge instructions are correct after aneurysm repair? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid lifting more than 10–15 lb for about 6–8 weeks or until cleared
Stop the beta blocker once BP is normal
Record BP and bring the log to visits
BANK.r: Teaching: take antihypertensives consistently (do NOT stop a beta blocker abruptly), BP log, stop smoking, no heavy lifting/straining, lifelong imaging, relatives screened.

BANK.q: Which symptom should prompt the client to call 911?
o: Sudden severe tearing back or abdominal pain
BANK.r: Call 911: sudden severe tearing abdominal, back, chest or head pain; fainting; new pulsating sensation.

BANK.q: Which lifestyle change most slows aneurysm expansion?
BANK.r: Smoking cessation is the highest-impact lifestyle change; with BP control it changes the trajectory most.

BANK.q: Which neurotransmitter is described as the brain's 'brake pedal'?
BANK.r: GABA is inhibitory and calming. Low GABA is linked to anxiety, panic and insomnia.

BANK.q: Which enzyme breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine?
BANK.r: MAO breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine. Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine.

BANK.q: Which neurotransmitters are INHIBITORY? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Inhibitory: GABA, glycine, serotonin. Excitatory: glutamate, epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, acetylcholine, histamine.

BANK.q: Low levels of which neurotransmitter cause anhedonia (inability to feel pleasure)?
BANK.r: Dopamine drives reward and motivation; low dopamine contributes to anhedonia.

BANK.q: A client took alprazolam with alcohol and is difficult to arouse with RR 8. Which reversal agent does the nurse anticipate?
BANK.r: IV flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine overdose. Benzos + other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids) → severe sedation and respiratory depression.

BANK.q: Which teaching is correct for a client prescribed diazepam? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants
Do not increase the dose on your own
Stop it abruptly when you feel better
Take it only on a strict schedule like buspirone
BANK.r: Benzo teaching: fall precautions, rise slowly, no dose increases, avoid depressants, taper slowly. Abrupt stop → withdrawal (anxiety, tremor, HTN, seizures).

BANK.q: How do benzodiazepines reduce anxiety?
o: Increase GABA activity in the CNS
BANK.r: Benzodiazepines are CNS depressants that increase GABA. Concerns: sedation, dependence/tolerance, hypotension, respiratory depression.

BANK.q: A client stops alprazolam abruptly. Which finding is MOST concerning?
BANK.r: Abrupt benzo withdrawal can cause anxiety, tremor, hypertension and seizures. Taper slowly.

BANK.q: A client asks to take buspirone 'only when I feel anxious.' Best response?
o: That is fine; it works within minutes
It must be taken on a regular schedule; the effect is delayed
Take two tablets during panic attacks
Take it with grapefruit juice for faster effect
BANK.r: Buspirone is NOT PRN: scheduled dosing, delayed therapeutic effect. Grapefruit juice increases levels; MAOIs can cause severe HTN.

BANK.q: How does buspirone differ from a benzodiazepine?
o: It does not depress the CNS and has less misuse concern
BANK.r: Buspirone: non-benzo, no CNS depression or misuse concern like benzos; scheduled, delayed onset. Adverse: dizziness, nausea, headache, paradoxical restlessness.

BANK.q: Which should the nurse monitor in a client starting fluoxetine? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Fluoxetine: monitor sodium (↑ADH → hyponatremia), weight, suicidal ideation, serotonin syndrome. Tyramine restriction is for MAOIs.

BANK.q: When should fluoxetine usually be taken?
o: Only with a fatty meal at night
BANK.r: Fluoxetine causes CNS excitation (insomnia, nervousness), so give in the morning. Clinical effect may take 4–6 weeks.

BANK.q: A client on fluoxetine takes daily ibuprofen. Which risk increases?
BANK.r: SSRIs + NSAIDs increase GI bleeding risk. SSRI within 2 weeks of an MAOI increases serotonin syndrome risk.

BANK.q: Which assessment is MOST important for a client on venlafaxine?
BANK.r: Venlafaxine (SNRI) blocks serotonin AND norepinephrine reuptake → hypertension. Monitor BP regularly and watch for weight loss.

BANK.q: A client wants to stop venlafaxine today. Which response is correct?
o: Stopping is safe at any time
It must be tapered over 2–4 weeks to prevent withdrawal
Double the dose for 1 day, then stop
BANK.r: Abrupt discontinuation → anxiety, agitation, headache, tachycardia. Taper over 2–4 weeks. Give with food; morning dosing.

BANK.q: Venlafaxine increases which neurotransmitters?
BANK.r: SNRI = serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Uses: depression, GAD, social anxiety disorder.

BANK.q: Which adverse effects are expected with amitriptyline? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: TCA blocks histamine (sedation) and acetylcholine (anticholinergic: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision) plus orthostatic hypotension. Give at bedtime.

BANK.q: A depressed client at risk for self-harm is prescribed amitriptyline. What is the priority nursing concern?
o: Overdose can cause life-threatening dysrhythmias; limit supply
It must be taken in the morning
BANK.r: TCA overdose is dangerous: fatal dysrhythmias, confusion, seizures. ATI: limit supply in clients at risk.

BANK.q: Which tip helps the anticholinergic effects of amitriptyline?
o: Sugar-free gum, water, fluids and fiber
BANK.r: Teach: gum/hard candy/water for dry mouth; fluids and fiber for constipation; rise slowly; take at bedtime; don't stop abruptly.

BANK.q: Bupropion is CONTRAINDICATED in a client with a history of:
BANK.r: Bupropion increases seizure risk. ATI contraindications: seizure disorder, history of eating disorder, concurrent MAOI.

BANK.q: Which apply to bupropion? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Bupropion: dopamine, activating (insomnia, agitation), weight loss, seizure risk; uses include depression, SAD prevention, smoking cessation; swallow SR/XR whole.

BANK.q: Which memory cue fits bupropion?
o: Think UP: activating, weight down, seizure risk up
Think DOWN: sedating and weight gain
BANK.r: Bupropion: more activating, appetite/weight may go down, seizure risk goes up.

BANK.q: A client on phenelzine has a sudden severe occipital headache and BP 210/120 after eating aged cheese. What is happening?
BANK.r: MAOIs block tyramine metabolism. Tyramine → norepinephrine release → vasoconstriction → hypertensive crisis. ATI treatment: IV phentolamine or SL nifedipine.

BANK.q: Which foods should a client taking phenelzine AVOID? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Avoid tyramine: aged cheese, aged/smoked meat, beer. Safer: fresh whole foods, fruits and vegetables.

BANK.q: Which statement about MAOIs is correct?
o: They are first-line for all depression
They are used for depression not responding to other classes
They are safe to combine with SSRIs
BANK.r: Phenelzine: depression unresponsive to other classes. SSRI + MAOI → serotonin syndrome. Adverse: orthostatic hypotension, insomnia, agitation.

BANK.q: A medication increases ADH. Which finding should the nurse watch for?
BANK.r: Increased ADH → fluid retention → hyponatremia (seen with SSRIs).

BANK.q: A medication blocks histamine. Which nursing action follows?
o: Fall precautions; bedtime dosing may help
BANK.r: Blocking histamine → drowsiness → fall/safety concern. CNS excitation is the one dosed in the morning.

BANK.q: Which side effect is a common reason antidepressant clients stop their medication?
BANK.r: Sexual dysfunction (SSRIs, SNRIs) is a common reason for nonadherence.

BANK.q: Which teaching applies to antidepressants in general? Select all that apply.
o: They can increase the risk of suicide, especially early
Double the dose if no effect after 2 days
BANK.r: Antidepressants take time; don't stop abruptly; can increase suicide risk early or with changes; monitor and report worsening.

BANK.q: A client on fluoxetine was recently started on another serotonergic drug and is agitated, confused, tremulous, sweating and febrile. What is the priority concern?
BANK.r: Too much serotonin = serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, tremor, sweating, fever, diarrhea. It's an emergency.

BANK.q: Which is the difference between serotonin syndrome and MAOI hypertensive crisis?
o: Too much serotonin vs tyramine/norepinephrine-driven severe hypertension
Both are caused by dopamine blockade
BANK.r: Serotonin syndrome = excess serotonin. Hypertensive crisis = tyramine → norepinephrine → vasoconstriction.

BANK.q: A client on lithium has a level of 1.0 mEq/L. How does the nurse interpret this?
BANK.r: Lecture therapeutic range 0.8–1.2 mEq/L; 1.5 mEq/L can cause toxicity. Narrow therapeutic range.

BANK.q: How does lithium reduce mania? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Lithium ↑ serotonin and GABA, ↓ dopamine and glutamate, and displaces intracellular sodium to reduce neuronal hyperactivity.

BANK.q: Which labs are monitored for a client on lithium? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Monitor serum lithium, sodium, kidney function, I&O and thyroid function.

BANK.q: Which are the EARLY signs of lithium toxicity?
BANK.r: Early toxicity: nausea + muscle weakness; fine tremor → coarse tremor. Progression: ataxia/confusion → seizures, coma, death.

BANK.q: Which instructions help prevent lithium toxicity? Select all that apply.
o: Drink about 2–3 L of fluid per day
Keep sodium intake consistent and moderate
BANK.r: The body handles lithium like sodium. Dehydration or low sodium → kidneys retain lithium → toxicity. NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines increase risk.

BANK.q: A client on lithium has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Why is the nurse concerned?
o: Dehydration and sodium loss can raise lithium levels
GI loss lowers lithium to subtherapeutic
No concern; lithium is not affected
BANK.r: Low water + low sodium = lithium rises. Check level and hydration.

BANK.q: A client began chlorpromazine yesterday and now has severe spasms of the neck and tongue. Which EPS is this?
BANK.r: Acute dystonia: hours to days after first dose. Parkinson-like: first month. Akathisia (restlessness): first 2 months. TD: months to years, possibly irreversible.

BANK.q: Which adverse effects are associated with chlorpromazine? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: 1st gen: blocks dopamine (EPS/TD), acetylcholine (anticholinergic), histamine (drowsiness), norepinephrine (hypotension/bradycardia); photosensitivity, dysrhythmias.

BANK.q: A client on a conventional antipsychotic for 3 years has lip smacking and tongue movements. This is:
BANK.r: Tardive dyskinesia: months to years; abnormal involuntary movements, potentially irreversible. More common with 1st-generation drugs.

BANK.q: Which should be monitored for a client on risperidone? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Atypicals increase appetite → weight gain, new/worsening diabetes, increased lipids. EPS less often than conventional drugs.

BANK.q: Risperidone mainly blocks:
BANK.r: 2nd generation: more serotonin blockade than dopamine. Treats positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, bipolar, irritability with autism.

BANK.q: A client on haloperidol has temp 104.2°F, severe muscle rigidity, BP swings and is confused. What is the nurse's priority?
o: Treat as NMS: stop the antipsychotic, cool and hydrate, notify provider
Give a PRN dose for agitation
Encourage fluids and recheck in 4 hours
BANK.r: NMS: high fever + rigidity + unstable VS + altered consciousness = emergency. Stop the drug, cool, hydrate; anticipate dantrolene and bromocriptine.

BANK.q: Which medications does ATI list for neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
BANK.r: NMS: prepare dantrolene + bromocriptine. Phentolamine/nifedipine treat MAOI hypertensive crisis.

BANK.q: Which glaucoma medication lowers IOP by DECREASING aqueous humor production?
BANK.r: Timolol (beta blocker) decreases production. Latanoprost, pilocarpine and echothiophate constrict the ciliary muscle → ↑ outflow.

BANK.q: Which teaching is specific to latanoprost?
o: It may darken iris, eyelid or eyelash pigment; give in the evening
It must be taken in the morning with food
BANK.r: Latanoprost (prostaglandin analog): evening dosing; iris/eyelid/eyelash pigmentation changes; eye irritation.

BANK.q: How do cholinergic drugs like pilocarpine increase aqueous outflow?
o: Constrict ciliary muscle/pupil, opening drainage canals
BANK.r: Pupil/ciliary constriction opens drainage canals → ↑ outflow → ↓ IOP.

BANK.q: Long-term echothiophate use is associated with:
BANK.r: Echothiophate (cholinesterase inhibitor): night vision decrease; cataracts with long-term use.

BANK.q: Which eye-drop instructions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Press on the inner corner of the eye (puncta) for at least 60 seconds
Wait at least 5 minutes between different eye drops
Touch the dropper tip to the eye to ensure delivery
Use extra caution with night driving
BANK.r: Punctal pressure ≥60 sec reduces systemic absorption. Remove contacts, don't touch the tip, separate drops by 5 min. Pupil constriction → poor low-light vision.

BANK.q: A client using pilocarpine reports dark floaters, flashes of light and a curtain over part of the vision. What should the nurse do?
o: Have the client rest the eyes for a week
BANK.r: With cholinergic glaucoma therapy, floaters, flashes or a curtain over vision suggest retinal detachment. Report.

BANK.q: Which systemic cholinergic effects can occur with pilocarpine? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Systemic cholinergic effects: urinary urgency, bradycardia, bronchoconstriction. Punctal pressure reduces absorption.

BANK.q: Which statement best defines clinical judgement?
o: The observed outcome of critical thinking and decision-making
BANK.r: Clinical judgement is the observed outcome of critical thinking and decision-making: an iterative process of observing, prioritizing, generating solutions, acting and reassessing.

BANK.q: Which is the correct order of the NCSBN Clinical Judgement Model?
o: Recognize cues → Analyze cues → Prioritize hypotheses → Generate solutions → Take action → Evaluate outcomes
Analyze cues → Recognize cues → Take action → Generate solutions → Prioritize → Evaluate
Take action → Evaluate → Recognize → Analyze → Prioritize → Generate
Prioritize → Recognize → Analyze → Generate → Evaluate → Take action
BANK.r: NOTICE → CONNECT → PRIORITIZE → PLAN → DO → CHECK.

BANK.q: Which factors influence a nurse's clinical judgement? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Influences: nurse experience, client situation, environment complexity, and content/nursing knowledge.

BANK.q: A nurse reviews the chart and notes HR 118, new confusion and a potassium of 3.1. Which clinical judgement step is the nurse performing?
BANK.r: Recognize cues = collect/filter relevant information from VS, labs, history, observations. Don't connect them to hypotheses yet.

BANK.q: Which question matches 'Recognize cues'?
BANK.r: Recognize: What do I notice? Analyze: What does it mean? Prioritize: What matters most? Generate: What could I do? Act: What will I do now? Evaluate: Did it work?

BANK.q: The nurse links a client's tachycardia, cool clammy skin and restlessness to possible hemorrhage. Which step is this?
BANK.r: Analyze cues = organize and link cues to the clinical presentation, find patterns, compare expected vs unexpected, consider what conditions fit.

BANK.q: What separates 'Recognize cues' from 'Analyze cues'?
BANK.r: Recognize = notice and filter data. Analyze = connect the data and interpret what it could mean; ask whether more information is needed.

BANK.q: The nurse decides that the client's possible bleeding is more urgent than their anxiety. Which step is this?
BANK.r: Prioritize hypotheses = rank possible problems by urgency, likelihood, risk; ask which is most likely and most serious; weigh risk of action vs inaction.

BANK.q: Which words in a test question usually point to 'Prioritize hypotheses'?
BANK.r: NCLEX clue: priority, first, most important, immediate, most likely point to prioritization.

BANK.q: The nurse lists expected outcomes and several possible interventions but has not done any yet. Which step is this?
BANK.r: Generate solutions = GOALS + OPTIONS. Identify outcomes, evidence-based interventions and resources. Additional assessment can itself be a solution.

BANK.q: What is the difference between Generate solutions and Take action?
o: Plan possible interventions vs actually implement them
BANK.r: Generate = plan options; Take action = carry out the priority intervention(s).

BANK.q: Which nursing behaviors belong to 'Take action'? Select all that apply.
o: Compare the client's response with the expected outcome
BANK.r: Take action verbs: administer, perform, notify, teach, document, collaborate. Comparing response to expected outcome = Evaluate.

BANK.q: While taking action, what should the nurse also consider?
o: Client preferences and the client's response
BANK.r: Use the specific scenario rather than a memorized routine; incorporate client preferences and needs; monitor the response.

BANK.q: After giving furosemide, the nurse reassesses lung sounds and compares them to the expected outcome. Which step is this?
BANK.r: Evaluate = compare observed response to expected outcome: improving, declining or unchanged? Reassess and revise the plan.

BANK.q: An expected outcome was NOT met. What happens next?
o: The clinical judgement cycle continues; reassess and modify the plan
Repeat the same action without reassessing
BANK.r: If the outcome isn't met, the cycle continues: reassess, modify outcomes or actions, update the plan of care.

BANK.q: Using ABCs, which client should the nurse see FIRST?
o: Client with stridor and drooling after a bee sting
BANK.r: When life is at stake: Airway, then Breathing, then Circulation. Stridor/drooling = airway threat.

BANK.q: Which client has the HIGHEST priority using ABCs?
o: Client with SpO2 86% and labored breathing
Client asking for a meal tray
BANK.r: Airway first, then breathing, then circulation. Labored breathing with low SpO2 is a breathing threat ahead of mild tachycardia or pain.

BANK.q: Using Maslow's hierarchy, which need is addressed FIRST?
BANK.r: Physiological needs generally come first, then safety & security, love & belonging, self-esteem, self-actualization.

BANK.q: Which client need ranks HIGHEST using Maslow?
o: Client who has not eaten or drunk in 2 days
Client who wants a support group
Client who feels embarrassed by a dressing
BANK.r: Physiological (food, water) before love/belonging and self-esteem.

BANK.q: The safety and risk-reduction framework asks the nurse to:
o: Identify which situation poses the greatest threat right now
BANK.r: Ask which finding poses the greatest threat now; compare risks rather than treating them equally; combine with ABCs or another framework if several are dangerous.

BANK.q: Several options all seem dangerous. What should the nurse do?
o: Combine safety with another framework such as ABCs
BANK.r: When several risks exist, combine safety/risk reduction with ABCs or another appropriate framework.

BANK.q: A client reports new chest discomfort. Before giving any PRN medication, what should the nurse do FIRST?
BANK.r: Nursing process: assessment/data collection comes before intervention when more information is needed to choose the right action.

BANK.q: Which list gives the RN nursing process in order?
o: Data collection, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation only
BANK.r: RN: 5 steps (Assessment, Analysis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation). PN uses 4 (Data collection, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation).

BANK.q: A client with mild dyspnea is sitting flat in bed. Using least restrictive/least invasive, the nurse should FIRST:
o: Raise the head of the bed
BANK.r: Choose the least restrictive or invasive intervention that still meets the need, before IV insertion, oxygen or medication when appropriate.

BANK.q: Which intervention is least restrictive for a confused client pulling at lines?
o: Frequent reorientation and a sitter at bedside
BANK.r: Use the least restrictive effective option before restraints or medication.

BANK.q: Which client should the nurse assess FIRST?
o: Client with chronic COPD and baseline SpO2 90%
Client with a stable diabetic foot ulcer
BANK.r: Acute > chronic, unstable > stable, urgent > nonurgent. A new, worsening or unexpected finding needs priority attention.

BANK.q: Which finding generally deserves closer priority?
o: A finding the client has had since childhood
BANK.r: New, worsening, unexpected or unstable findings take priority over chronic expected ones.

BANK.q: In a mass-casualty event, a client has a life-threatening injury with HIGH survival potential once stabilized. Which class?
BANK.r: Class I: life-threatening but survivable with stabilization; highest priority. II: major but not immediately life-threatening. III: minor. IV: unlikely to survive; comfort care.

BANK.q: In mass-casualty triage, a client with injuries unlikely to be survived receives:
BANK.r: Class IV Expectant: comfort measures rather than restorative care. Triage prioritizes survival potential and limited resources.

BANK.q: How is mass-casualty triage different from ordinary priority questions?
o: It focuses on survival potential and use of limited resources
It always treats the sickest first
BANK.r: Ordinary priority = individual urgency. Mass casualty = survival potential/resource allocation.

BANK.q: Which neurotransmitter does the lecture emphasize in eating disorders?
BANK.r: Serotonin pathways are disrupted; low serotonin reduces satiety. Carbohydrate binges may be an attempt to restore serotonin.

BANK.q: Which are risk factors for eating disorders? Select all that apply.
o: Elite athletics, dance, modeling or wrestling
Older age with no other factors
BANK.r: Risks: genetic/family history, perfectionism, OCD, low self-esteem, trauma, media pressure, appearance-focused sports, weight teasing, family over-involvement.

BANK.q: Eating disorders are often underreported because of:
o: Secrecy, denial and avoidance of treatment
BANK.r: Secrecy, denial and avoidance lead to underreporting. They affect every body system and carry elevated suicide risk.

BANK.q: Which are early warning signs of an eating disorder? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Warning signs: unexplained weight change, severe dieting, ritualized mealtime behavior, lying about intake, body-image preoccupation, compulsive exercise.

BANK.q: A client has lost 15 lb unexpectedly. What does the course say to do before assuming an eating disorder?
o: Rule out medical causes of weight change
BANK.r: Don't assume an eating disorder from weight change alone; rule out medical causes first.

BANK.q: Which approach is best when taking a nursing history from a client suspected of an eating disorder?
o: Calm, nonjudgmental; compare report with observations and labs
Confront the client with the weight
BANK.r: Ask the client's perception, eating habits, weight-control methods; denial can be part of the disorder, so compare with observations and labs.

BANK.q: Which findings are expected in a client with anorexia nervosa? Select all that apply.
o: Enlarged parotid glands with Russell's sign
BANK.r: Anorexia: weight <85% expected, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo, dry/yellow skin, amenorrhea, decreased bone density. Russell's sign and parotids = bulimia.

BANK.q: A client with anorexia has constipation, lanugo, HR 42 and BP 82/48. Which finding is the PRIORITY?
BANK.r: Cardiovascular instability comes before less-urgent findings: bradycardia + hypotension + dysrhythmias before constipation.

BANK.q: A significantly underweight client binges and purges. Which diagnosis fits best?
BANK.r: Purging + significantly underweight → anorexia binge/purge type. Normal or above weight with binge/purge → bulimia.

BANK.q: A client says, 'If I eat any dessert, I'll gain 50 pounds.' Which distortion is this?
BANK.r: All-or-nothing: one dessert = 50 lb. Personalization: 'everyone is looking at me.' Emotional reasoning: 'I feel bloated so I look bad.'

BANK.q: 'I know I look bad because I feel bloated' is an example of:
BANK.r: Emotional reasoning uses a feeling as proof. Catastrophizing: 'My life is over if I gain weight.'

BANK.q: How should the nurse respond to a client's distorted body image statements?
o: Prove the client is thin with a mirror
BANK.r: Don't argue about the distortion; acknowledge feelings and avoid power struggles.

BANK.q: Which findings are hallmarks of bulimia nervosa? Select all that apply.
o: Calluses or scars on the knuckles (Russell's sign)
BANK.r: Bulimia: Russell's sign, parotid swelling, dental erosion, sore throat, esophageal tears, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis. Weight usually normal or slightly above.

BANK.q: A client with bulimia suddenly reports severe chest pain and vomits blood. What does the nurse suspect?
o: Serious GI injury such as esophageal tear; urgent attention
BANK.r: Sudden severe chest/abdominal pain or vomiting blood can indicate esophageal tear or gastric rupture; urgent.

BANK.q: What is the frequency criterion for bulimia nervosa?
o: At least once weekly for 3 months
Once a month for a year
BANK.r: Bulimia and BED: binges at least once weekly for 3 months, with loss of control.

BANK.q: Which feature distinguishes binge eating disorder from bulimia?
BANK.r: BED: recurrent binges + loss of control + marked distress, but NO purging or excessive exercise. Often overweight/obese.

BANK.q: Which complications are associated with binge eating disorder? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: BED complications: T2DM, HTN, hyperlipidemia, heart disease, gallbladder disease, sleep apnea, arthritis.

BANK.q: A client of normal weight binges, then exercises for hours to 'undo it.' Which disorder fits?
BANK.r: Fast test: 1) weight? 2) compensate after binge? Normal weight + compensation (exercise/fasting counts) = bulimia.

BANK.q: Which disorder has NO FDA-approved medication in the course materials?
BANK.r: Anorexia: none. Bulimia: fluoxetine. BED: lisdexamfetamine.

BANK.q: An obese client reports eating large amounts rapidly when not hungry, alone, then feeling disgust. No purging. Which disorder?
BANK.r: Binge without compensation + distress = BED. Loss of control and significant distress separate it from ordinary overeating.

BANK.q: Which acid-base imbalance results from repeated self-induced vomiting?
BANK.r: Vomiting loses ACID from the TOP → metabolic alkalosis (↑HCO3). Laxatives lose BASE from the BOTTOM → metabolic acidosis.

BANK.q: Which electrolyte does the lecture emphasize as the priority because it can cause fatal dysrhythmias?
BANK.r: Low K+ from vomiting/laxatives/diuretics → weakness and dysrhythmias. Potassium is the priority electrolyte.

BANK.q: A client misusing laxatives has a low bicarbonate. Which imbalance is this?
BANK.r: Laxative diarrhea loses base → metabolic acidosis.

BANK.q: Which lab findings can occur in eating disorders? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Also anemia/leukopenia, increased liver enzymes, abnormal thyroid/glucose. Vomiting LOWERS potassium.

BANK.q: Which findings meet hospitalization criteria for a client with an eating disorder? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Hospitalize: weight ≤75% IBW, HR <50, SBP <90, temp <35.5°C/95.9°F, ECG changes, electrolyte disturbances, refusal to eat, suicidal behavior, failed outpatient care.

BANK.q: A severely underweight client has HR 44 and K+ 2.8 and wants to start group therapy today. What comes first?
BANK.r: Physical stabilization before psychological work.

BANK.q: Which nursing actions are appropriate for a hospitalized client with bulimia? Select all that apply.
o: Stay with the client during and after meals
Accompany to the bathroom after meals
Weigh daily, same time, same scale, same clothing
Assess suicide risk at every contact
Let the client exercise freely after meals
BANK.r: Supervise meals and bathroom, watch for hidden food, limit excessive exercise, consistent daily weights (morning after voiding), I&O, potassium, cardiac rhythm, suicide risk.

BANK.q: What weekly weight gain goal does the course give?
BANK.r: Course goal: 2–3 lb per week, with behavioral contracts and rewards for positive behavior.

BANK.q: Why offer the client choices in the plan of care?
o: To provide a sense of control
To let the client skip meals
BANK.r: Clients often feel out of control; appropriate choices give a sense of control. Build trust through consistency.

BANK.q: Which nutrition measures are appropriate during refeeding of a client with anorexia? Select all that apply.
o: Low sodium to reduce fluid retention
BANK.r: Work with dietitian: structured schedule, small frequent meals, liquid supplements, high fiber, low sodium, limit high-fat/gassy foods early, multivitamin, avoid caffeine.

BANK.q: Which therapy is especially used for ADOLESCENTS with anorexia?
BANK.r: Family-based therapy for adolescents. CBT is emphasized for bulimia and BED.

BANK.q: Which electrolytes drop in refeeding syndrome?
BANK.r: Carbs → insulin → P, K and Mg shift INTO cells → blood levels drop: hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia.

BANK.q: Which actions help prevent refeeding syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Baseline and daily phosphorus, potassium, magnesium and glucose
Start feeding slowly (10–20 kcal/kg/day) and advance gradually
Give thiamine before feeds as ordered
Give a large high-carbohydrate meal first
BANK.r: Identify at-risk clients, check labs, start slow, thiamine, cardiac monitoring, watch for fluid overload.

BANK.q: When is the risk of refeeding syndrome highest?
BANK.r: Highest risk in the first 24–72 hours. Manifestations: weakness, confusion, seizures, dysrhythmias, HF, respiratory distress, edema.

BANK.q: Which clients are AT RISK for refeeding syndrome? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: At risk: severe anorexia, chronic alcohol use, prolonged fasting/starvation, significant weight loss, NPO >7 days.

BANK.q: Which teaching is correct for fluoxetine prescribed for bulimia? Select all that apply.
o: Take it with an MAOI for better effect
BANK.r: Fluoxetine: only FDA-approved drug for bulimia; morning dosing; 1–4 weeks; don't stop abruptly; black box suicidality <25 yr; never combine with MAOI.

BANK.q: Per the course slide, how long must a client wait after stopping fluoxetine before starting an MAOI?
BANK.r: Wait 14 days after an MAOI before fluoxetine; wait 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before an MAOI.

BANK.q: Fluoxetine's black box warning is about:
o: Increased suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents and adults under 25
BANK.r: Black box: increased suicidal thoughts/behaviors under 25, especially early and with dose changes.

BANK.q: Which apply to lisdexamfetamine for binge eating disorder? Select all that apply.
o: Schedule II with abuse/misuse black box
Take once daily in the morning
BANK.r: Lisdexamfetamine: CNS stimulant; ↑ dopamine/norepinephrine; first FDA-approved for moderate–severe BED in adults; NOT approved for weight loss; combine with CBT.

BANK.q: A client on lisdexamfetamine reports chest pain and fainting. The nurse should:
o: Tell the client this is expected
BANK.r: Report chest pain, SOB, fainting, hallucinations or tics. Avoid caffeine/alcohol; store securely; don't share.

BANK.q: Which nurse statement is MOST therapeutic for a client with anorexia who finished lunch?
o: 'I noticed you finished your lunch today. How are you feeling about that?'
BANK.r: Avoid comments about appearance or weight, even positive ones. Focus on feelings and behaviors.

BANK.q: Before working with a client with an eating disorder, what should the nurse do first?
o: Read the client's diet diary aloud
Set a weigh-in in front of peers
BANK.r: Self-assess your own feelings first to maintain a nonjudgmental approach; be consistent across staff.

BANK.q: Which age range shows the largest increase in eating disorder symptoms?
BANK.r: Largest symptom increase ages 12–15. ARFID is more than picky eating and is not driven by body image.

BANK.q: Which clue may suggest an eating disorder in a male client?
o: Excessive weight training, supplements or anabolic steroids
BANK.r: Males are often underdiagnosed; may pursue muscularity rather than thinness.

BANK.q: What is hydronephrosis?
o: Swelling of the kidney from backed-up urine
A kidney stone in the urethra
BANK.r: Blockage → urine backs up → pressure rises → hydronephrosis/hydroureter → GFR falls → waste builds → possible renal damage; stagnant urine raises infection risk.

BANK.q: Which findings are expected with hydronephrosis? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Hydronephrosis: flank pain, N/V, fever if infected, reduced UO. Main test: ultrasound. Care: relieve obstruction, pain control, antibiotics if infected, monitor kidney function.

BANK.q: Which can cause urinary obstruction? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Causes: stones, tumors, strictures, BPH, neurogenic bladder, trauma.

BANK.q: Which kidney stone type is the MOST common?
BANK.r: Calcium ~80% (calcium oxalate; diet/oxalate). Struvite ~10% (UTI). Uric acid ~9% (gout). Cystine ~1% (inherited cystinuria).

BANK.q: A client with recurrent urinary tract infections is most at risk for which stone?
BANK.r: Struvite stones are associated with UTIs.

BANK.q: A client with gout passes a dark, tea-colored stone. Which type is likely?
BANK.r: Uric acid stones: gout; dark tea-colored stone.

BANK.q: A client has acute, wave-like flank pain radiating toward the groin, urgency and hematuria. Where is the stone most likely?
BANK.r: Ureter: acute colicky, wave-like flank pain + urgency. Renal pelvis: deep costovertebral ache. Bladder: irritation, retention, hematuria.

BANK.q: A deep, dull costovertebral ache suggests a stone in the:
BANK.r: Renal pelvis stone → deep costovertebral ache.

BANK.q: Which conservative measures are used for a client passing a kidney stone? Select all that apply.
o: Strain ALL urine and save the stone
BANK.r: Conservative: hydrate as ordered, analgesics, tamsulosin, strain all urine and save stone for analysis.

BANK.q: After ESWL (lithotripsy), which finding is expected?
o: Flank bruising and stone fragments in strained urine
Bright red urine with clots for days
BANK.r: ESWL uses shock waves to break stones; strain urine afterward; flank bruising may occur. Report fever, absent UO, worsening pain.

BANK.q: Which procedure uses a small back incision to remove a large, complex kidney stone?
BANK.r: PCNL: small back incision for large/complex stones; monitor the tube and bleeding. URS: scope through urethra/bladder.

BANK.q: A client with a ureteral stent reports fever and no urine output for 4 hours. The nurse should:
o: Give an extra dose of tamsulosin
BANK.r: Report fever, restricted/absent UO, worsening pain or signs of infection/obstruction promptly.

BANK.q: Which prevention teaching fits a client with calcium oxalate stones? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Prevention: hydration, adjust diet by stone type, avoid excess salt, oxalate guidance for calcium oxalate, follow-up.

BANK.q: Why must the client save a passed stone?
BANK.r: Stone analysis identifies the type so diet and prevention can be tailored.

BANK.q: Which are OBSTRUCTIVE symptoms of BPH? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Obstructive: hesitancy, weak stream, straining, dribbling, incomplete emptying. Irritative: urgency, frequency, nocturia.

BANK.q: On digital rectal exam, BPH typically feels:
BANK.r: BPH = smooth enlarged prostate. Nodules or hard areas suggest prostate cancer. PSA assesses for cancer.

BANK.q: Which are risk factors for BPH in the lecture? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: BPH risks: age >50, family history, hormonal changes, obesity/sedentary, diabetes/heart disease, high-fat diet.

BANK.q: How does tamsulosin relieve BPH symptoms?
BANK.r: Alpha blockers (tamsulosin, terazosin) RELAX. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) SHRINK the prostate over time.

BANK.q: Which teaching helps a client with BPH? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid large fluid intake in the evening
Take OTC cold medicine for congestion
BANK.r: Decongestants and antihistamines can worsen retention. Avoid caffeine/alcohol and large evening fluids; timed voiding.

BANK.q: Which medication shrinks the prostate over time?
BANK.r: Finasteride (5-alpha reductase inhibitor) shrinks. Combination therapy for moderate–severe symptoms.

BANK.q: After TURP with continuous bladder irrigation, the drainage has turned darker red with a few small clots. Per protocol, the nurse should FIRST:
o: Increase the irrigation rate per protocol
BANK.r: CBI goal: light pink → clear. Darker drainage or small clots → increase irrigation per protocol. If bright red drainage or large clots persist, assess and notify the provider.

BANK.q: A client on CBI reports bladder spasms and the abdomen is distended with little drainage. FIRST action?
o: Check the tubing for kinks or obstruction
BANK.r: Distention or pain → check tubing for obstruction/kinks first.

BANK.q: How is true urine output calculated during CBI?
BANK.r: Actual urine output = total drainage − irrigant infused.

BANK.q: Which post-TURP instruction is correct?
o: Avoid straining, heavy lifting and strenuous exercise
BANK.r: Avoid straining, heavy lifting and strenuous exercise per instructions; monitor bleeding and infection.

BANK.q: Which test CONFIRMS prostate cancer?
BANK.r: DRE may find nodules; PSA may be elevated; biopsy confirms. MRI/CT/bone scan evaluate spread.

BANK.q: A client's Gleason score is 9. What does this mean?
BANK.r: Gleason 2–10: higher score = more aggressive. Stage describes extent of spread.

BANK.q: Which are prostate cancer risk factors on the slides? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Risks: age >50, family history, African-American ancestry, obesity, high-fat diet.

BANK.q: After radical prostatectomy, which should the nurse monitor? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Post-op: catheter and pain care, incontinence, erectile dysfunction, psychosocial support.

BANK.q: Oliguria is defined in the lecture as urine output less than:
BANK.r: Oliguria <400 mL/24 hr. Anuria: very little/no urine (up to 50 mL/24 hr in lecture).

BANK.q: What is the difference between azotemia and uremia?
o: Azotemia = nitrogen waste in blood; uremia = waste buildup WITH symptoms
Azotemia = urea crystals on the skin
BANK.r: Azotemia: nitrogen waste in the blood. Uremia: azotemia with symptoms. Uremic frost: urea crystals on the skin.

BANK.q: Which are normal kidney functions? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Kidneys: filter waste, form urine, fluid/electrolytes, acid-base, BP, RBC production (EPO), activate vitamin D, clear drugs, secrete prostaglandins.

BANK.q: Which lab change meets the lecture's AKI criterion?
o: Creatinine rises by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours
BANK.r: AKI: serum creatinine rises ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours. Rapid loss of function over hours to days.

BANK.q: A client develops AKI after hemorrhagic shock. Which type of AKI is this?
BANK.r: Prerenal = too little blood to the kidney (dehydration, hemorrhage, burns, shock). Intrarenal = direct tissue damage. Postrenal = blocked outflow.

BANK.q: AKI from an enlarged prostate blocking urine flow is classified as:
BANK.r: Postrenal: mechanical urinary obstruction (ties back to Week 8.1).

BANK.q: AKI from direct glomerular or tubular injury is:
BANK.r: Intrarenal affects the renal cortex or medulla directly.

BANK.q: During which AKI phase do oliguria, azotemia, fluid retention and metabolic acidosis develop?
BANK.r: Initiation: insult to injury (hours–days). Maintenance: GFR drops, oliguria, azotemia, fluid retention, electrolyte imbalance, acidosis (often 1–2 weeks). Recovery: GFR improves; diuresis; up to a year.

BANK.q: A client recovering from AKI suddenly has a large increase in urine output. Which phase?
BANK.r: Recovery: tubular repair, GFR returns, diuresis can occur; may persist up to one year.

BANK.q: A 70-kg post-op client has had 25 mL/hr of urine for 3 hours. What does the nurse do?
o: Recognize possible AKI; assess perfusion and notify the team
BANK.r: UO <0.5 mL/kg/hr (35 mL/hr for 70 kg) for >2 hr may signal AKI. Act early; waiting for 6 hours of oliguria can let damage progress. Keep MAP >65.

BANK.q: Which history findings raise a client's risk for AKI? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Risks: older age, diabetes, CKD, surgery, shock, dehydration; review NSAIDs, antibiotics, contrast.

BANK.q: Which findings suggest fluid overload in AKI? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Fluid overload: crackles, dependent/generalized edema (anasarca), weight gain. Monitor I&O, daily weights, lung sounds.

BANK.q: Which are indications for renal replacement therapy in AKI? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: RRT for symptomatic uremia, K+ >6.5, severe acidosis (pH <7.1) or fluid overload that inhibits tissue perfusion.

BANK.q: A client with low urine output may need a fluid challenge. What should the nurse do FIRST?
BANK.r: Assess fluid status before assuming low UO needs more fluid. A fluid challenge (500–1000 mL NS over 1 hr) is prescribed, not routine for everyone.

BANK.q: Which interventions help prevent or limit AKI? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid nephrotoxic agents including contrast when possible
Check kidney function before imaging with contrast
BANK.r: Prevent hypotension, maintain fluid balance, avoid nephrotoxins, review drug doses, dietitian for nutrition.

BANK.q: What are the two LEADING causes of CKD?
BANK.r: DM and HTN lead. Also heart disease, older age, obesity, glomerulonephritis, inherited disorders. African Americans are at greater risk.

BANK.q: A client's GFR is 12 mL/min/1.73 m². Which CKD stage?
Which describes CKD vs AKI?
o: CKD: progressive, irreversible, >3 months; AKI: rapid, may recover
BANK.r: AKI develops rapidly and may recover. CKD lasts >3 months, is progressive/irreversible and affects ALL body systems.

BANK.q: A client's GFR is 25 mL/min/1.73 m². Which stage?
BANK.r: Stage 4: 15–29 — severe waste buildup, impaired homeostasis.

BANK.q: Why do clients with CKD develop anemia?
BANK.r: Decreased EPO → anemia. Also impaired platelet function (bleeding) and reduced immunity (infection).

BANK.q: Which lab is the PRIORITY in a client with kidney failure because it can cause fatal dysrhythmias?
BANK.r: Potassium can become life-threatening. Monitor K+, cardiac rhythm, fluid overload; escalate critical findings.

BANK.q: Which GI findings are expected with CKD/uremia? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Uremia affects the whole GI system: halitosis, stomatitis, anorexia, N/V, hiccups, peptic ulcer disease.

BANK.q: Per the lecture, protein needs for a client with CKD change how once dialysis begins?
BANK.r: Before dialysis ≈0.8 g/kg/day; protein needs increase once dialysis begins (≈1–1.3 g/kg/day).

BANK.q: Which belong in a CKD diet as prescribed? Select all that apply.
o: Limit phosphorus; phosphate binders if needed
Count fluid-containing foods toward the fluid limit
BANK.r: Renal diet: limit Na, K, phosphorus; fluid restriction counting fluid-containing foods; avoid sodas high in phosphorus; dietitian.

BANK.q: Which antacids does the lecture say to AVOID in kidney failure?
BANK.r: Avoid magnesium-containing antacids; review doses of antibiotics, opioids, insulin and other renally cleared drugs.

BANK.q: Which medication is given to correct anemia from CKD?
BANK.r: Epoetin alfa (ESA) stimulates RBC production.

BANK.q: Which medication slows the progression of CKD?
BANK.r: SGLT2 inhibitor dapagliflozin (Farxiga) slows CKD progression. ACEI/ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure.

BANK.q: Why are ACE inhibitors or ARBs used in CKD?
o: Reduce intraglomerular pressure and protect the kidney
BANK.r: ACEI/ARBs reduce intra-glomerular pressure; BP control is essential.

BANK.q: When are loop or thiazide diuretics useful in CKD?
o: To manage volume overload while the kidney still makes urine
BANK.r: Diuretics increase UO to manage overload when elimination is still present.

BANK.q: Which assessment confirms an AV fistula is patent?
o: Absent pulse distal to the site
BANK.r: Check thrill (vibration) and bruit (whoosh). Report absent thrill/bruit or uncontrolled bleeding immediately.

BANK.q: For a client with a left-arm AV fistula, which actions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: No BP readings in the left arm
No venipuncture or IVs in the left arm
Assess thrill and bruit every shift
Use the left arm for lab draws to save veins
BANK.r: Access = lifeline: no BP, no needles, no IVs in the access arm.

BANK.q: What is the MOST common complication during or after hemodialysis?
BANK.r: HD: hypotension most common; also cramps, headache, N/V, bleeding, access infection. Peritonitis = PD.

BANK.q: Which pre/post hemodialysis assessments are appropriate? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: HD: weight, VS, bleeding, hypotension; medication holding per orders. Effluent = PD.

BANK.q: A client on peritoneal dialysis has cloudy effluent and abdominal pain. What does the nurse suspect?
BANK.r: PD: think PERITONITIS + strict exchange I&O. Report abnormal effluent or drainage problems.

BANK.q: Which are true about peritoneal dialysis? Select all that apply.
o: The peritoneum acts as the membrane
Often fewer diet and fluid restrictions than HD
BANK.r: PD: abdominal catheter (CAPD, IPD, APD), sterile technique, record inflow/dwell/outflow, fewer restrictions, strict schedule.

BANK.q: Which technique is essential for PD catheter and exit-site care?
o: Use the site for IV access
BANK.r: Sterile technique for catheter/exit site; monitor pre/post VS and weight.

BANK.q: A 3-year-old is admitted with a suspected Wilms tumor. Which nursing action is the PRIORITY?
o: Post a sign: DO NOT palpate the abdomen
Give a warm tub bath with abdominal massage
BANK.r: Suspected Wilms tumor = NEVER palpate the abdomen. Protect the abdomen during handling and bathing.

BANK.q: Which findings are associated with Wilms tumor? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Wilms (nephroblastoma): abdominal mass, pain, hematuria, HTN, fever, poor appetite, weight loss; lung spread → cough/dyspnea.

BANK.q: Which statement about radiation for Wilms tumor matches the lecture?
o: It is used for inoperable or too-large tumors and avoided in young children
It is given to every child before surgery
BANK.r: Treatment: neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemo, nephrectomy (partial or total); radiation for inoperable/too-large tumors, avoided in young children.

BANK.q: Which are risk factors for renal cell carcinoma? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: RCC risks: smoking, obesity, HTN, genetic factors, CKD, long-term dialysis.

BANK.q: Which classic findings suggest renal cell carcinoma?
o: Hematuria, flank pain and abdominal mass
BANK.r: RCC: hematuria + flank pain + mass; fatigue, fever, anemia, weight loss. Most common kidney cancer (from renal tubular epithelium).

BANK.q: Which RCC treatment preserves the kidney for a small tumor (<4 cm) or a non-surgical candidate?
BANK.r: Ablation preserves the kidney for tumors <4 cm or non-surgical candidates. Nephrectomy (partial, total, radical) is emphasized; arterial embolization may precede surgery.

BANK.q: A 68-year-old who smoked for 40 years reports blood in the urine with no pain. What does the nurse suspect?
BANK.r: Painless hematuria = consider bladder cancer. Smoking is the greatest risk.

BANK.q: Which are risk factors for bladder cancer? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Risks: smoking (greatest), toxic gas/diesel, chemicals, certain drugs (phenacetin, cyclophosphamide), schistosomiasis, recurrent UTI, radiation.

BANK.q: After a cystectomy with ileal conduit, what is the nursing priority?
BANK.r: After diversion: prioritize urine drainage + stoma/skin integrity; watch for leakage, obstruction, infection.

BANK.q: Which intravesical therapy is used for bladder cancer?
BANK.r: Intravesical immunotherapy: BCG (and others). Also cystectomy, chemo, radiation.

BANK.q: Adequate perfusion depends on three components. Which set is correct?
BANK.r: Pump (cardiac output = HR × SV), volume (circulating blood), conduit (intact vessels). An aneurysm is a weak spot in the conduit.

BANK.q: Cardiac output is calculated as:
BANK.r: CO = HR × stroke volume. Rupture lowers volume → preload → stroke volume → CO.

BANK.q: A 60-kg client's urine output was 22 mL in the last hour. How does the nurse interpret this?
o: Below the 0.5 mL/kg/hr marker; renal perfusion may be falling
BANK.r: 0.5 × 60 = 30 mL/hr minimum. 22 mL/hr is below the bedside marker of renal perfusion.

BANK.q: A true aneurysm is defined as permanent dilation of:
o: More than 50% or 1.5× the normal diameter
BANK.r: True aneurysm: >50% or >1.5× original diameter, all three layers (intima, media, adventitia) stretched but intact.

BANK.q: Which aneurysm shape is typical of a cerebral 'berry' aneurysm?
BANK.r: Saccular = outpouching on one side (cerebral berry). Fusiform = circumferential (abdominal aorta).

BANK.q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: An aortic dissection is not the same as an aneurysm
A dissection is a dilated but intact wall
A pseudoaneurysm involves all three layers intact
BANK.r: Aneurysm = dilation. Dissection = tear + false lumen; an acute emergency.

BANK.q: Which intervention most directly reduces aneurysm wall tension?
BANK.r: Tension = pressure × radius. The nurse can't change radius quickly, but BP control lowers pressure.

BANK.q: Which are perfusion consequences of a failing aneurysm wall? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Local: embolization (mural thrombus). Systemic: massive hemorrhage → severe hypoperfusion → shock.

BANK.q: Which history findings increase a 64-year-old man's risk of AAA? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Age >60, male, smoking, HTN, family history, hyperlipidemia/atherosclerosis, stimulants, obesity, sedentary lifestyle.

BANK.q: Which recreational drug use raises aneurysm risk?
BANK.r: Stimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine) are modifiable risk factors via BP spikes.

BANK.q: Who should discuss aneurysm screening with their provider?
o: First-degree relatives of a client with an aneurysm
BANK.r: Family history is a risk; first-degree relatives should discuss screening.

BANK.q: Where is an AAA most commonly located?
BANK.r: AAA is usually infrarenal and silent until large or ruptured. About 65% of aneurysms are abdominal aortic.

BANK.q: An AAA is found incidentally on CT. Most AAAs are:
BANK.r: Most AAAs are asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging.

BANK.q: A client's 4.2 cm AAA grew 0.3 cm in 6 months. What is the expected plan?
o: Surveillance imaging, BP/lipid control, smoking cessation
BANK.r: Under 5.5 cm and growth under 0.5 cm in 6 months: watchful waiting with serial ultrasound and risk-factor control.

BANK.q: Hoarseness in a client with a TAA is caused by:
BANK.r: The aneurysm compresses the laryngeal nerve. Dysphagia = esophageal compression; dyspnea = airway pressure.

BANK.q: Which are major complications of a thoracic aortic aneurysm? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: TAA complications: rupture, dissection, aortic insufficiency/regurgitation, thromboembolism.

BANK.q: For a client with a suspected TAA, where should BP be taken?
BANK.r: Assess BP in both arms; unequal pressures can suggest dissection.

BANK.q: What is the most common peripheral aneurysm?
BANK.r: Popliteal fossa is the most common peripheral site; often bilateral. Others: femoral, carotid, subclavian/brachial.

BANK.q: A client with a popliteal aneurysm reports lower-leg numbness and swelling. What explains this?
BANK.r: Nerve compression → numbness/weakness; vein compression → edema.

BANK.q: Which findings signal limb ischemia from a peripheral aneurysm? Select all that apply.
o: Warm pink foot with brisk refill
BANK.r: Thromboembolism → pain, pallor, diminished/absent pulse, cool mottled limb.

BANK.q: Which study is the GOLD STANDARD for aneurysm size, shape and surgical planning?
BANK.r: CTA is the gold standard; check renal function and contrast allergy and hydrate.

BANK.q: A client is scheduled for a transesophageal echo (TEE) to assess the aortic root. Which nursing action is needed?
o: Keep NPO before; monitor airway after sedation
BANK.r: TEE: NPO beforehand; monitor airway after sedation.

BANK.q: What is the FIRST study for a suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured cerebral aneurysm?
BANK.r: Non-contrast CT head first; lumbar puncture if CT is negative.

BANK.q: A ruptured AAA may show which skin finding on the flank?
BANK.r: Ruptured: cool, pale, diaphoretic skin; possible flank ecchymosis.

BANK.q: What determines survival after a ruptured AAA?
o: Rapid recognition and immediate surgical repair
BANK.r: Mortality is very high; survival depends on recognition and immediate repair (large-bore IVs, crossmatch, OR/EVI).

BANK.q: Which parameters should the nurse trend to catch compensated shock early? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Trend mentation, pulses, skin, UO, HR and pulse pressure; don't wait for hypotension.

BANK.q: Which medications are SECOND-line BP agents for a stable aneurysm?
o: ACE inhibitors, ARBs or calcium channel blockers
BANK.r: First line: beta blockers (labetalol, esmolol). Second line: ACEI (lisinopril), ARB (losartan), CCB (amlodipine).

BANK.q: What is the heart rate goal when a beta blocker is used for an aneurysm?
BANK.r: Beta blockers lower HR (goal 60–70) and force of ejection, lowering wall stress.

BANK.q: Which therapies may be added for atherosclerotic disease in a client with an aneurysm?
BANK.r: Statins (atorvastatin) and antiplatelet therapy (aspirin with clopidogrel, ticagrelor or prasugrel) as appropriate.

BANK.q: Which repair is generally associated with a longer ICU stay and more blood loss?
BANK.r: Open: cross-clamp, sewn graft, more blood loss, longer ICU stay, greater physiologic stress.

BANK.q: Which requirement limits who can receive EVAR?
BANK.r: EVAR requires suitable vessel anatomy; lifelong surveillance for endoleak.

BANK.q: After EVAR, what does an endoleak mean?
o: Persistent blood flow into the aneurysm sac
BANK.r: Endoleak = persistent flow into the sac after EVAR; needs lifelong imaging.

BANK.q: Why does the nurse palpate and mark peripheral pulses before aneurysm repair?
o: To have a baseline for post-op comparison
BANK.r: Marked baseline pulses let the nurse detect a new deficit (graft occlusion/embolism) after surgery.

BANK.q: What monitoring is used for strict BP titration pre-op?
BANK.r: Arterial line for continuous BP; titrate antihypertensive infusions per protocol.

BANK.q: How should the nurse document vital signs for an aneurysm client?
o: As trends rather than isolated values
BANK.r: Monitor VS and perfusion markers closely and document trends.

BANK.q: Which pulmonary and GI care is part of post-op aneurysm management? Select all that apply.
o: Keep on strict bed rest for 2 weeks
BANK.r: Incentive spirometry, early mobility, monitor bowel function; ileus is a known complication.

BANK.q: After repair, which finding suggests acute kidney injury?
o: Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hr with rising creatinine
BANK.r: AKI can follow contrast, hypoperfusion or cross-clamping. Track hourly UO, daily weights, BUN/Cr.

BANK.q: Every complication after aneurysm repair is ultimately a problem of:
BANK.r: Find the organ downstream and ask whether it is receiving blood.

BANK.q: Which statement shows the client understands aneurysm teaching?
o: 'I'll keep a BP log and bring it to every appointment.'
'I can stop my labetalol when I feel fine.'
BANK.r: BP log, consistent meds, lifelong imaging, lifting limits.

BANK.q: Which should be reported after discharge from aneurysm repair? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden severe chest or back pain
BANK.r: Report S/S of infection, peripheral ischemia; call 911 for sudden severe pain, fainting or new pulsating sensation.

BANK.q: Why should a client avoid straining at stool after aneurysm repair?
o: Valsalva raises pressure on the graft and vessel
BANK.r: Avoid straining/Valsalva and heavy lifting; stool softeners may be used.

BANK.q: Which receptor receives acetylcholine?
BANK.r: Cholinergic receptors receive acetylcholine. Adrenergic receive epinephrine/norepinephrine.

BANK.q: How can medications change neurotransmitter activity? Select all that apply.
o: Block the enzyme that breaks it down
BANK.r: Agonists stimulate, antagonists block, and enzyme or reuptake blockers keep more transmitter around.

BANK.q: Excess glutamate is linked to:
BANK.r: Glutamate is the most abundant excitatory transmitter; too much → excitotoxicity, seizures, mood disorders.

BANK.q: Which neurotransmitter manages the fight-or-flight response?
BANK.r: Norepinephrine/epinephrine trigger alertness and fight-or-flight; tied to anxiety, PTSD, ADHD.

BANK.q: Diazepam may be used for which conditions? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Diazepam: anxiety, muscle spasm/spasticity, status epilepticus, alcohol withdrawal, anesthesia induction.

BANK.q: An older adult on a benzodiazepine becomes more agitated and confused. This is called:
BANK.r: Paradoxical confusion/anxiety can occur. Other effects: drowsiness, slurred speech, impaired recall, hypotension, respiratory depression.

BANK.q: Which benzodiazepine is especially associated with dependence and tolerance in the lecture?
BANK.r: Dependence/tolerance is especially important with alprazolam.

BANK.q: Which drink should a client on buspirone avoid?
BANK.r: Grapefruit juice can increase buspirone levels.

BANK.q: Which adverse effects can occur with buspirone? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Buspirone: dizziness/lightheadedness, nausea, headache, paradoxical insomnia/anxiety/restlessness. No CNS depression.

BANK.q: A client on phenelzine is prescribed buspirone. What is the concern?
BANK.r: MAOI + buspirone can cause severe hypertension.

BANK.q: Fluoxetine is used for which conditions? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Fluoxetine: major depression, bipolar depression, panic disorder, OCD, PMDD, bulimia.

BANK.q: A client on fluoxetine reports a headache and confusion; sodium is 128 mEq/L. What explains this?
BANK.r: SSRIs increase ADH → fluid retention → hyponatremia. Monitor sodium.

BANK.q: How long may fluoxetine take to reach full clinical effect per the pharm notes?
BANK.r: Fluoxetine may take 4–6 weeks for clinical effectiveness (eating disorder notes say 1–4 weeks for bulimia).

BANK.q: Which adverse effects are associated with venlafaxine? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Venlafaxine: N/V/anorexia, headache, HTN, insomnia/nervousness, suicidal ideation.

BANK.q: How should venlafaxine be taken to reduce GI upset?
BANK.r: Give with food for GI effects; morning dosing reduces sleep interference.

BANK.q: Venlafaxine is used for which conditions? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: SNRI uses: major depression, GAD, social anxiety disorder.

BANK.q: When should amitriptyline be given?
BANK.r: Sedating (blocks histamine) → bedtime dosing.

BANK.q: Which findings suggest TCA overdose? Select all that apply.
o: Bradycardia with constricted pupils from cholinergic excess
BANK.r: TCA overdose: life-threatening dysrhythmias, confusion, seizures.

BANK.q: Which receptors does amitriptyline block, explaining its side effects?
BANK.r: Blocks histamine (drowsiness) and acetylcholine (anticholinergic); also increases serotonin and norepinephrine.

BANK.q: A client on bupropion reports hearing voices. The nurse should:
o: Report it; psychosis is a possible adverse effect
BANK.r: Bupropion adverse effects include psychosis/hallucinations/delusions and suicidal ideation.

BANK.q: Why is bupropion avoided in a client with a history of an eating disorder?
BANK.r: ATI contraindications: seizure disorder, eating disorder history, MAOI use.

BANK.q: Which seasonal use is listed for bupropion?
BANK.r: Uses: depression, SAD prevention, smoking-cessation adjunct.

BANK.q: Which explanation of MAOI hypertensive crisis is correct?
o: Tyramine isn't broken down → norepinephrine release → vasoconstriction
BANK.r: MAO also metabolizes tyramine; with MAO blocked, tyramine rises and triggers norepinephrine release.

BANK.q: Which treatment does ATI list for MAOI hypertensive crisis?
BANK.r: Hypertensive crisis: IV phentolamine or sublingual nifedipine.

BANK.q: Which adverse effect is common with phenelzine?
BANK.r: Phenelzine: orthostatic hypotension, anxiety/insomnia/agitation, GI effects, suicidal ideation.

BANK.q: A drug produces CNS excitation. Which teaching fits?
BANK.r: CNS excitation → insomnia, nervousness, headache, elevated BP; morning dosing helps.

BANK.q: Which effects come from blocking acetylcholine? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Anticholinergic: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision (and orthostatic hypotension per slides).

BANK.q: An antipsychotic blocks norepinephrine. Which findings follow?
BANK.r: Blocking norepinephrine → BP/HR effects; lecture emphasizes hypotension and bradycardia.

BANK.q: Which findings fit serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, tremor, sweating, fever, diarrhea. Emergency.

BANK.q: When is suicide risk highest with antidepressants?
o: Early in treatment or when therapy changes
BANK.r: Monitor for worsening depression/suicidal ideation especially early or with dose changes.

BANK.q: How long should a client wait after stopping an MAOI before starting an SSRI?
BANK.r: SSRI within 2 weeks of an MAOI increases serotonin syndrome risk.

BANK.q: Lithium is used primarily for:
BANK.r: Lithium is the main treatment for bipolar disorder; controls manic episodes.

BANK.q: A client's lithium level is 1.6 mEq/L. Interpretation?
BANK.r: Therapeutic example 0.8–1.2; 1.5 can cause toxicity.

BANK.q: Why is lithium described as having a 'narrow therapeutic range'?
o: Small difference between effective and toxic levels
It works in a narrow age group
BANK.r: Narrow range → frequent level monitoring.

BANK.q: A client on lithium has coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion. What does the nurse suspect?
BANK.r: Fine tremor/GI upset may occur; coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion signal toxicity progressing toward seizures.

BANK.q: Which drugs can increase lithium toxicity risk? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: NSAIDs (not aspirin), tetracyclines, diuretics, ACE inhibitors and others raise lithium levels.

BANK.q: A client on lithium has GI upset. Which tip helps?
o: Take it with food or milk
BANK.r: Take with food or milk for GI upset; maintain fluids and consistent sodium.

BANK.q: A client on chlorpromazine for 6 weeks paces constantly and can't sit still. Which EPS?
BANK.r: Akathisia = restlessness; may occur within the first 2 months.

BANK.q: Chlorpromazine may be used for which conditions? Select all that apply.
o: Acute manic phase of bipolar disorder
BANK.r: Chlorpromazine uses: schizophrenia, acute mania, N/V, intractable hiccups.

BANK.q: A client on chlorpromazine plans a beach vacation. Which teaching applies?
o: Use sunscreen and protective clothing; photosensitivity
BANK.r: Chlorpromazine causes photosensitivity.

BANK.q: A client with diabetes starts risperidone. What should the nurse anticipate?
BANK.r: Atypicals increase appetite → weight gain, new/worsening diabetes, increased lipids.

BANK.q: Risperidone is used for which conditions? Select all that apply.
o: Positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia
BANK.r: Risperidone: schizophrenia (positive + negative), bipolar, irritability with autism.

BANK.q: Compared with chlorpromazine, risperidone causes EPS:
o: Less often, mainly at higher doses
BANK.r: EPS at higher doses but less often than conventional agents; main concerns are metabolic.

BANK.q: What separates NMS from tardive dyskinesia?
o: NMS is acute fever + rigidity + unstable VS; TD is chronic abnormal movements
BANK.r: TD: chronic, months–years. NMS: acute, rare, life-threatening.

BANK.q: Which findings fit neuroleptic malignant syndrome? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: NMS: high fever + rigidity + unstable VS + altered/lost consciousness.

BANK.q: Which supportive care is part of NMS management?
BANK.r: Stop/urgent management, cooling, hydration; prepare dantrolene + bromocriptine.

BANK.q: Glaucoma damages the optic nerve because of:
BANK.r: Excess aqueous production and/or decreased outflow → ↑ IOP → optic nerve damage → peripheral vision loss/blindness.

BANK.q: Which medications lower IOP by INCREASING aqueous outflow? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Latanoprost, pilocarpine, echothiophate → ciliary constriction → ↑ outflow. Timolol ↓ production.

BANK.q: How does echothiophate work?
o: Inhibits the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine
BANK.r: Cholinesterase inhibitor → more acetylcholine → ciliary constriction → ↑ outflow.

BANK.q: Why does the nurse press on the inner corner of the eye after glaucoma drops?
BANK.r: Punctal (nasolacrimal) pressure for at least 60 seconds reduces systemic absorption.

BANK.q: A client uses two different eye drops. How long should they wait between them?
BANK.r: Separate ophthalmic medications by at least 5 minutes.

BANK.q: Which safety concern comes from pupil constriction with glaucoma drops?
BANK.r: Constricted pupils → poor low-light vision → nighttime safety precautions.

BANK.q: Why is content knowledge alone NOT enough for clinical judgement?
o: The nurse must apply it to the client's actual situation
BANK.r: Clinical judgement applies knowledge to the real client; it's iterative: observe, prioritize, act, reassess.

BANK.q: Which teaching strategies help develop clinical judgement? Pick the BEST answer.
o: Unfolding case studies, simulation with debriefing, written reflection
BANK.r: Deliberate practice, case studies, unfolding cases, simulation/debriefing, care plans, reflection.

BANK.q: Which sources does the nurse filter during 'Recognize cues'? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Recognize cues: signs/symptoms, history, record, VS, labs, prescriptions, observations, environment, client perspective.

BANK.q: A client's chart shows many findings. During 'Recognize cues,' the nurse's main task is to:
BANK.r: Identify relevant vs irrelevant info and what is of immediate concern.

BANK.q: While analyzing cues, the nurse realizes she needs a fingerstick glucose before deciding. This reflects:
o: Asking whether additional information is needed
BANK.r: Analyze: link cues, compare expected vs unexpected, consider conditions, decide if more information is needed.

BANK.q: Which question best fits 'Analyze cues'?
BANK.r: Analyze = what does it mean; patterns and relationships.

BANK.q: During 'Prioritize hypotheses,' the nurse weighs:
BANK.r: Cluster info, establish priority by urgency, likelihood, risk; consider risk of action vs inaction.

BANK.q: Which two questions define 'Prioritize hypotheses'?
o: Which is most likely? Which is most serious?
What did I notice? What did I do?
Who is on shift? When is lunch?
Did it work? Should I chart it?
BANK.r: Most likely and most serious guide ranking.

BANK.q: Which belong in 'Generate solutions'? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Generate = goals + options + resources + what to avoid. Administering = Take action.

BANK.q: Can additional assessment be a 'solution' in the Generate solutions step?
o: Yes; more data collection can be a possible solution
No; assessment is only in step 1
